title: Mole Concept and Stoichiometry
tagline: Apply mole relationships, gas laws and chemical equations to quantitative calculations.

overview.intro: The mole concept provides a bridge between the microscopic world of atoms and molecules and measurable quantities such as mass and gas volume. Stoichiometry uses balanced chemical equations to relate amounts of reactants and products. In ICSE Class 10, students apply Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes, Avogadro’s law, relative atomic and molecular masses, molar volume of gases, percentage composition, and empirical and molecular formulae to solve numerical problems.

learningOutcomes: State Gay-Lussac’s law and Avogadro’s law and apply them to gaseous reactions.
Define mole, molar mass and molar volume and interconvert mass, moles and particles.
Calculate relative molecular mass and percentage composition from formulae.
Determine empirical and molecular formulae from composition data.
Solve stoichiometric problems using balanced chemical equations.

blocks.text: Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes states that when gases react, they do so in volumes which bear a simple whole-number ratio to one another and to the volumes of gaseous products, provided all volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. This law supports the idea that gas volumes reflect the number of reacting particles.

Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. From this follows the concept of molar volume: one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litres at standard temperature and pressure (STP), a value commonly used in ICSE calculations.

items.note: Simple whole-number volume ratio illustrates Gay-Lussac’s law.

items.text: If 2 L of oxygen contains N molecules at STP, then 2 L of nitrogen also contains N molecules at STP.
items.note: Equal volumes imply equal numbers of molecules under identical conditions.

learn.title: The Mole, Molar Mass and Molar Volume

blocks.text: A mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.022 × 10^23 elementary entities (atoms, molecules or ions). The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative atomic or molecular mass and is called molar mass. These relationships allow conversion between mass, number of moles and number of particles.

For gases, one mole occupies 22.4 L at STP, so volume can be related to moles and mass. Care must be taken to use consistent units and to distinguish between atoms and molecules when counting particles, especially for diatomic gases such as O2 and H2.

learn.title: Percentage Composition, Empirical and Molecular Formulae

blocks.text: Percentage composition expresses the mass percentage of each element in a compound. It is calculated from the formula by dividing the total mass contributed by each element in one mole of the compound by the molar mass and multiplying by 100. Such calculations are useful for verifying purity and understanding composition.

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of elements in a compound, while the molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms in a molecule. To find the molecular formula, determine the empirical formula mass and compare it with the molecular mass: molecular formula = (empirical formula) × n, where n is an integer.

items: Convert percentage composition to moles by dividing by atomic masses.
Simplify mole ratios to the smallest whole numbers for empirical formula.
Use molecular mass to scale empirical formula to molecular formula.
Show clear steps: ratio, simplification, and final formula.

blocks.text: A balanced chemical equation gives the mole ratio in which reactants combine and products form. These ratios can be used to calculate masses or volumes of substances involved in a reaction. For gaseous reactions, volume ratios at the same temperature and pressure are the same as mole ratios.

Stoichiometric problems should be approached systematically: write and balance the equation, convert given quantities to moles, use the mole ratio from the equation, and convert back to the required unit. When a reactant is in excess, the limiting reactant concept may be implied, though basic ICSE problems often provide sufficient information directly.

items.meaning: Calculation of reactants and products in chemical reactions using balanced equations.
Mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole.
Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of elements in a compound.

blocks.text: Accuracy in mole calculations depends on correct atomic masses, proper balancing of equations and consistent units. Rounding should be done appropriately, usually at the final step, to avoid cumulative errors. When using gas volumes, ensure conditions are stated as STP or equivalent as assumed in the problem.

Students should clearly label each step: finding molar mass, calculating moles, applying ratios and stating the final answer with units. This structured approach reduces mistakes and earns method marks in examinations even when arithmetic slips occur.

items.text: To find moles in 11 g of CO2 (molar mass 44 g/mol): n = 11/44 = 0.25 mol.
items.note: Direct application of n = mass/molar mass.

items.text: 0.5 mol of a gas at STP occupies 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 L.
items.note: Use molar volume for gaseous substances.

questions.prompt: One mole of any substance contains:
questions.answer: 6.022 × 10^23 particles
questions.explanation: Avogadro’s number defines the number of entities in one mole.
questions.commonMistake: 22.4 L is molar volume for gases at STP, not number of particles.

questions.prompt: The volume occupied by 1 mole of a gas at STP is:
questions.explanation: Molar volume of a gas at STP is taken as 22.4 litres in ICSE problems.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse 11.2 L (0.5 mole) with molar volume.

questions.prompt: The number of moles in 18 g of water (H2O, molar mass 18 g/mol) is:
questions.answer: 1 mol
questions.explanation: Number of moles = mass/molar mass = 18/18 = 1 mol.
questions.commonMistake: Divide mass by molar mass, not multiply.

questions.prompt: According to Avogadro’s law, equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal:
questions.answer: numbers of molecules
questions.explanation: Avogadro’s law relates gas volume directly to number of molecules under identical conditions.
questions.commonMistake: Different gases have different masses even if volumes and molecule counts are equal.

questions.prompt: The empirical formula of a compound with molecular formula C2H6 is:
questions.answer: CH3
questions.explanation: The simplest whole-number ratio of C:H in C2H6 is 1:3, so the empirical formula is CH3.
questions.commonMistake: Simplify subscripts by their highest common factor.

questions.prompt: Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes applies to:
options: gases reacting at same temperature and pressure
questions.answer: gases reacting at same temperature and pressure
questions.explanation: The law states simple volume ratios for gaseous reactants and products under identical conditions.
questions.commonMistake: Temperature and pressure must be the same for the volume ratios to hold.

questions.prompt: If 2 moles of CO2 are produced, the volume at STP is:
questions.explanation: Volume at STP = number of moles × 22.4 L = 2 × 22.4 = 44.8 L.
questions.commonMistake: Multiply moles by molar volume to get total volume.

questions.prompt: A compound has empirical formula CH2 and molecular mass 56. Its molecular formula is:
questions.answer: C4H8
questions.explanation: Empirical formula mass of CH2 is 14. n = 56/14 = 4, so molecular formula is C4H8.
questions.commonMistake: Find n by dividing molecular mass by empirical formula mass.

questions.prompt: The mass of one mole of a substance is called its ________ mass.
questions.answer: molar
questions.explanation: Molar mass is the mass of one mole, usually expressed in grams per mole.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse molar mass with relative mass without units.

questions.prompt: At STP, 0.5 mole of oxygen gas occupies ________ litres.
questions.explanation: Volume = 0.5 × 22.4 L = 11.2 L at STP.
questions.commonMistake: Use 22.4 L as the molar volume at STP.

questions.prompt: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound is given by its ________ formula.
questions.answer: empirical
questions.explanation: Empirical formula represents the simplest ratio, while molecular formula shows actual numbers.
questions.commonMistake: Molecular formula may be a multiple of the empirical formula.

questions.prompt: State Avogadro’s law.
questions.answer: Avogadro’s law states that equal volumes of all gases, under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules.
questions.explanation: The law links gas volume to number of molecules when conditions are identical.
questions.commonMistake: Include the condition of same temperature and pressure.

questions.prompt: Calculate the number of moles in 44 g of carbon dioxide (CO2). (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.answer: Molar mass of CO2 = 12 + (16 × 2) = 44 g/mol. Number of moles = 44/44 = 1 mole.
questions.explanation: Using n = mass/molar mass gives the amount of substance.
questions.commonMistake: Calculate molar mass correctly before dividing.

questions.prompt: Find the percentage of oxygen in water (H2O). (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: Molar mass of H2O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18 g/mol. Mass of oxygen = 16 g. Percentage of oxygen = (16/18) × 100 = 88.89% (approximately).
questions.explanation: Percentage composition is based on mass contribution relative to molar mass.
questions.commonMistake: Use total molar mass in the denominator.

questions.prompt: What volume of hydrogen at STP is required to react completely with 11.2 L of chlorine at STP to form HCl?
questions.answer: The reaction is H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. By Gay-Lussac’s law, 1 volume of H2 reacts with 1 volume of Cl2. Therefore, 11.2 L of hydrogen is required to react completely with 11.2 L of chlorine at STP.
questions.explanation: Equal reacting volumes follow the 1:1 mole/volume ratio in the balanced equation.
questions.commonMistake: Use the balanced equation to determine the volume ratio.

questions.prompt: Calculate the empirical formula of a compound containing 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen and 53.33% oxygen by mass. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: Assume 100 g of compound: C = 40 g, H = 6.67 g, O = 53.33 g. Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.67/1 = 6.67, O = 53.33/16 = 3.33. Divide by smallest (3.33): C = 1, H = 2, O = 1. The empirical formula is CH2O.
questions.explanation: Converting mass percentages to mole ratios gives the simplest whole-number formula.
questions.commonMistake: Divide each mole value by the smallest mole value to simplify the ratio.

questions.prompt: A gas has vapour density 22. Find its molecular mass and the volume occupied by 11 g of the gas at STP.
questions.answer: Molecular mass = 2 × vapour density = 2 × 22 = 44. Number of moles in 11 g = 11/44 = 0.25 mol. Volume at STP = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 L. Thus the molecular mass is 44 and the volume occupied is 5.6 L.
questions.explanation: Vapour density relates to molecular mass, which then allows mole and volume calculations.
questions.commonMistake: Remember molecular mass is twice vapour density.

questions.prompt: Calculate the mass of calcium oxide formed when 50 g of calcium carbonate is completely decomposed. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16). Equation: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
questions.answer: Molar mass of CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + (16 × 3) = 100 g/mol. Molar mass of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 g/mol. From the equation, 100 g CaCO3 produces 56 g CaO. Therefore, 50 g CaCO3 produces (56/100) × 50 = 28 g of CaO.
questions.explanation: The balanced equation gives a 1:1 mole ratio, allowing direct mass proportion calculation.
questions.commonMistake: Use molar masses from the balanced equation, not arbitrary ratios.

questions.prompt: 4.4 g of a gas occupies 2.24 L at STP. Calculate its molar mass and identify whether it could be CO2. (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.answer: Number of moles = volume/22.4 = 2.24/22.4 = 0.1 mol. Molar mass = mass/moles = 4.4/0.1 = 44 g/mol. Molar mass of CO2 = 12 + 32 = 44 g/mol, so the gas could be carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: Combining volume-to-mole conversion with mass gives molar mass for comparison.
questions.commonMistake: Ensure the volume used corresponds to STP when applying 22.4 L/mol.

questions.prompt: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen. Its vapour density is 21. Determine its empirical and molecular formulae. (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.answer: Moles: C = 85.7/12 = 7.14, H = 14.3/1 = 14.3. Ratio C:H = 7.14:14.3 = 1:2, so empirical formula is CH2 (empirical mass 14). Molecular mass = 2 × 21 = 42. n = 42/14 = 3. Molecular formula = C3H6.
questions.explanation: Empirical formula comes from composition; molecular formula uses vapour density.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse empirical mass with molecular mass when finding n.

questions.prompt: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to form ammonia: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. If 5.6 L of nitrogen reacts completely at STP, calculate the volume of hydrogen required and the volume of ammonia formed.
questions.answer: From the equation, 1 volume N2 reacts with 3 volumes H2 to give 2 volumes NH3. For 5.6 L N2: hydrogen required = 3 × 5.6 = 16.8 L, ammonia formed = 2 × 5.6 = 11.2 L (all at STP).
questions.explanation: Gas volume ratios at the same conditions follow the mole ratios in the balanced equation.
questions.commonMistake: Apply the ratio to each gas separately using nitrogen as reference.

questions.prompt: Explain why 2 g of hydrogen and 32 g of oxygen occupy the same volume at STP, and state that volume.
questions.answer: Molar mass of H2 is 2 g/mol, so 2 g is 1 mole. Molar mass of O2 is 32 g/mol, so 32 g is 1 mole. By Avogadro’s law, equal moles (and thus equal numbers of molecules) of gases occupy equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure. Therefore both occupy 22.4 L at STP.
questions.explanation: Equality of moles explains equality of volumes despite different masses.
questions.commonMistake: Equal masses of different gases do not occupy equal volumes; equal moles do.
